title: Neurological Vascular Disease
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how the brain and spinal cord are injured when blood flow stops, when vessels rupture, or when venous drainage or autoregulation fails. It covers ischemic infarction and its evolution under the microscope, global hypoxic injury, the four intracranial hemorrhages, vascular malformations, arterial dissection and subclavian steal, spinal cord infarction, venous sinus thrombosis, and posterior reversible encephalopathy. Board questions usually give a patient, a time course, an image description, or a tissue finding and ask for the vessel, the mechanism, or the next complication. If you can tie each lesion to the vessel that fails, the pressure behind it, and the space it fills, most of these questions become anatomy problems.
prerequisites: Circle of Willis and the territories of the anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries (NE-10)
Meninges, dural venous sinuses, and CSF production and absorption (NE-4)
Spinal cord tracts and where each decussates (NE-3, NE-5)
Glutamate receptors and neuronal membrane potential (NE-13)

connections.to: CNS blood supply and CSF flow (NE-10)

Hypertension drives lacunes, Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms, and PRES, while atherosclerosis and dissection cause large artery strokes.

terms.def: An area of tissue necrosis caused by loss of its blood supply.
Tissue around an infarct core that is electrically silent from reduced flow but still viable if flow returns.
Bleeding into an infarct when blood reenters vessels whose walls were damaged by ischemia.
A small cavitated infarct, less than about 15 mm across, from occlusion of a deep penetrating artery.
Necrosis in which enzymatic digestion turns dead tissue into fluid, typical of the brain.
Neuronal death caused by excess glutamate overstimulating receptors and loading the cell with Ca2+.
Infarction at the far ends of two adjacent arterial territories, where perfusion pressure is lowest.
A thin-walled outpouching at an arterial branch point of the circle of Willis, lacking media and internal elastic lamina in the sac.
Yellow discoloration of CSF from bilirubin formed as red cells in the subarachnoid space break down.
A tiny dilation of a small penetrating artery weakened by chronic hypertension.
Arteriolar constriction and dilation that hold cerebral blood flow nearly constant across a range of arterial pressure.
Extracellular brain edema from blood-brain barrier leak, in contrast to cytotoxic edema from cell swelling.

blocks.text: The brain receives about 15% of the cardiac output and uses about 20% of resting oxygen, yet it stores almost no glucose or glycogen. When an artery closes, function in its territory stops within seconds and irreversible injury begins within minutes. How the artery closes predicts the onset, the vessel, and the appearance of the infarct.

Thrombotic infarction occurs where a thrombus forms on an ulcerated or fissured atherosclerotic plaque. Plaques gather where flow is turbulent and shear stress is low, so the classic sites are the carotid bifurcation (origin of the internal carotid artery), the middle cerebral artery (MCA), and the basilar artery. Narrowing progresses slowly while collaterals partly compensate, so the deficit often develops in a stuttering or stepwise pattern. Because the vessel usually stays occluded, the infarct is typically pale (anemic).

Embolic infarction occurs when material formed elsewhere lodges in a cerebral artery. Most emboli are cardiac: left atrial appendage thrombus in atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus after myocardial infarction or in dilated cardiomyopathy, and vegetations on diseased valves. Artery-to-artery emboli from carotid plaque and paradoxical emboli through a patent foramen ovale also occur. The MCA is the usual destination because it continues the straight course of the internal carotid artery. The deficit is maximal at onset. Emboli often fragment or lyse within hours to days, and blood returning to vessels whose walls are already ischemic leaks into the infarct, producing hemorrhagic (red) conversion, often as petechiae along the cortex.

Lacunar infarcts arise in small penetrating arteries, such as the lenticulostriate branches of the MCA and the paramedian branches of the basilar artery, which leave large vessels at right angles and are exposed to near full arterial pressure. Chronic hypertension, and diabetes to a lesser degree, cause hyaline arteriolosclerosis: plasma proteins leak into the wall, the lumen narrows, and the vessel finally closes. Because these arteries supply densely packed tracts and nuclei, a lesion only millimeters wide can cause a pure motor stroke (posterior limb of the internal capsule) or a pure sensory stroke (ventral posterior thalamus), without cortical signs such as aphasia or neglect.

blocks.title: Three mechanisms of ischemic infarction
rows: Clot or vegetation from heart or proximal artery
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of a penetrating artery
Often hemorrhagic, may be multiple territories
blocks.caption: The mechanism of occlusion predicts onset, location, and whether the infarct becomes hemorrhagic.

blocks.predict: Why does an embolic infarct often become hemorrhagic while a thrombotic infarct usually stays pale?
blocks.explain: The embolus fragments or lyses and flow returns into vessels whose walls are already necrotic, so blood leaks into the tissue. A thrombus on a plaque usually keeps the artery occluded, so no blood reaches the damaged bed.

blocks.text: The appearance of an infarct follows the order of events after ATP fails: neurons die first, dead tissue attracts neutrophils, macrophages remove the debris, and astrocytes seal off what is left. The timing is predictable, so the microscopic findings date the infarct.

For the first several hours little is visible, even though neurons may already be irreversibly injured. By about 12 to 24 hours the typical sign is the red neuron (acute ischemic neuronal change): the cell body shrinks, the cytoplasm becomes intensely eosinophilic as Nissl substance (rough endoplasmic reticulum) is lost, and the nucleus becomes small and dark (pyknotic). Edema develops at the same time, first cytotoxic as failing ion pumps let cells swell, then vasogenic as damaged capillaries leak. Swelling is greatest within the first few days, which is when a large MCA infarct can cause herniation.

Neutrophils enter during the first few days. Macrophages, derived from blood monocytes and activated microglia, then take over and dominate for weeks. Myelin is rich in lipid, so these cells fill with lipid and become foamy macrophages (gitter cells); in a hemorrhagic infarct they also hold hemosiderin. Reactive astrocytes enlarge and multiply at the margin from about the end of the first week.

The end result differs from infarction in the heart or kidney, where coagulative necrosis preserves tissue outlines and fibroblasts lay down collagen. Brain parenchyma has abundant lipid and lysosomal enzymes, little supporting collagen, and almost no fibroblasts. Digestion therefore liquefies the dead tissue (liquefactive necrosis), and over weeks to months the infarct becomes a fluid-filled cyst crossed by small vessels and walled by a glial scar of astrocyte processes (gliosis) rather than a collagen scar.

blocks.title: Time course of an ischemic cerebral infarct
rows: Red neurons; cytotoxic then vasogenic edema
Pale, soft, swollen; gray-white junction indistinct
Macrophages (microglia and monocytes) become foamy as they clear myelin
blocks.caption: Times are approximate and vary with infarct size and source; the order of events is what boards test.

sections.title: Ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, and transient ischemic attack

blocks.text: About 85% of strokes are ischemic (thrombotic, embolic, or lacunar, as in C01) and about 15% are hemorrhagic, divided between intraparenchymal hemorrhage (C07) and subarachnoid hemorrhage (C06). Ischemic stroke injures tissue by withdrawing oxygen and glucose. Hemorrhagic stroke injures it by mass effect, raised intracranial pressure, and the toxic effects of blood, so it more often brings early headache, vomiting, and declining consciousness, although examination alone cannot reliably separate the two.

Normal cerebral blood flow is about 50 mL per 100 g of brain per minute. When an artery closes, flow in the center of its territory falls so low that ion pumps fail and cells die within minutes (the infarct core). Around the core, collateral flow keeps tissue alive but electrically silent; this ischemic penumbra causes part of the early deficit and can recover if flow returns, or join the infarct if it does not.

A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a brief episode of focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal dysfunction caused by ischemia without infarction on imaging. Most resolve within an hour. The current definition is tissue based: if MRI shows an infarct, the event is a stroke even when the symptoms disappear. A TIA indicates an unstable source, such as an ulcerated carotid plaque or a cardiac thrombus, and stroke risk is highest in the first days after it. Transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) from emboli to the ophthalmic artery is a retinal TIA that points to the ipsilateral carotid artery.

The two types share risk factors because both reflect vessel wall damage. Age is the strongest nonmodifiable factor and hypertension the strongest modifiable one, driving atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis, and microaneurysm rupture. Atrial fibrillation supplies emboli, diabetes and dyslipidemia accelerate atherosclerosis, and smoking injures endothelium.

Noncontrast CT is the first image because it answers the question that changes everything: is there blood? Fresh blood is bright (hyperdense) on CT at once, because a clot packs hemoglobin and protein densely. Early ischemia, by contrast, often looks normal for the first several hours, then shows loss of gray-white differentiation and, over about a day, a dark (hypodense) territory. Contrast is omitted because enhancing vessels are also bright and could hide or mimic blood. A clot-dissolving drug given into a hemorrhage would enlarge it, which is why blood must be excluded before reperfusion is considered. MRI diffusion imaging detects ischemic cell swelling within minutes but takes longer to obtain.

blocks.predict: A patient has right arm weakness for 40 minutes that resolves completely, but MRI shows a small acute infarct in the left internal capsule. TIA or stroke?
blocks.explain: Stroke. The tissue-based definition depends on infarction, not on how long symptoms last.

sections.title: Global hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and watershed infarcts

blocks.text: Global hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy results when the whole brain loses its supply of oxygen, as in cardiac arrest, shock, severe hypotension, drowning, or carbon monoxide poisoning. Consciousness is lost within about 10 seconds of absent flow, and in a normothermic adult, irreversible neuronal injury begins after about 4 to 5 minutes. Ischemia (no flow) is more harmful than hypoxia with preserved flow, because flow still delivers glucose and removes lactate and other metabolites.

blocks.title: Excitotoxic neuronal injury
steps: Oxygen and glucose delivery stop
ATP falls and Na+/K+ ATPase fails
Neurons depolarize and release glutamate; reuptake fails
NMDA receptor activation floods neurons with Ca2+
Ca2+ activates proteases, phospholipases, and free radical production
Membranes and cytoskeleton break down; neuron dies
blocks.caption: This cascade drives both focal infarction and global hypoxic injury; neurons with the most glutamate input are lost first.

blocks.text: Neurons are more vulnerable than glia, and some neurons are more vulnerable than others. The classic sites are pyramidal neurons of hippocampal sector CA1 (Sommer sector), cerebellar Purkinje cells, and pyramidal neurons of the neocortex. These cells receive heavy glutamatergic input, have high metabolic demand, and handle Ca2+ loads poorly. Hippocampal injury explains the severe anterograde memory loss of many survivors of cardiac arrest, and CA1 neurons can die over the following days (delayed neuronal death). In the cortex, damage is selective for the deeper layers 3, 5, and 6, producing bands of necrosis parallel to the surface called pseudolaminar (laminar) necrosis. Severe injury leaves widespread cortical loss and can end in a persistent vegetative state or brain death.

Watershed (border zone) infarcts form where two arterial territories meet. These regions lie at the farthest ends of both arterial trees, so their perfusion pressure is lowest. A fall in systemic pressure starves them first, even when no artery is blocked. The ACA and MCA border zone is most affected: a sickle-shaped strip over the convexity a few centimeters lateral to the midline, which contains the motor cortex for the proximal arm and shoulder (and hip). Bilateral lesions give proximal limb weakness with sparing of the face and hands, sometimes called man in a barrel. The MCA and PCA border zone in the parieto-occipital region causes visual and higher cortical deficits.

blocks.predict: After a cardiac arrest, a patient has bilateral weakness of the shoulders and upper arms with normal hand grip and facial movement. Where is the lesion and why there?
blocks.explain: Bilateral ACA and MCA watershed zones. The shoulder and proximal arm are represented on the upper convexity, between the medial ACA strip (leg) and the lateral MCA region (hand and face), at the ends of both arterial trees, where pressure fell most.

blocks.text: The dura is the key to both lesions. Its outer layer is the periosteum of the inner skull and is bound most tightly at the sutures; its inner surface faces the arachnoid across a potential space crossed by bridging veins. Each hematoma takes its shape and speed from the vessel that tears and the space the blood must open.

Epidural hematoma lies between skull and dura and is usually arterial. The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery that enters through the foramen spinosum, runs in a groove on the inner surface of the thin squamous temporal bone near the pterion. A fracture there tears it, and blood at arterial pressure strips the dura from bone. The dura holds firm at the sutures, so the clot bulges inward as a biconvex (lens-shaped) collection that does not cross sutures. The patient is often briefly knocked out by the impact, may then recover for minutes to hours (the lucid interval), and then deteriorates as the clot expands. It is uncommon in older adults, whose dura is more firmly attached to the skull.

blocks.title: From temporal fracture to herniation
steps: Temporal bone fracture tears the middle meningeal artery
Arterial blood strips dura from bone, stopping at sutures
Brief unconsciousness, then a lucid interval in some patients
Expanding biconvex clot raises intracranial pressure
Uncus herniates and compresses CN III and midbrain
Coma, brainstem compression, and death if pressure is not relieved
blocks.caption: Arterial pressure makes the epidural clot grow over hours, so decline after the lucid interval is rapid.

blocks.text: Subdural hematoma is usually venous. Bridging veins pass from the cortical surface to the dural sinuses, chiefly the superior sagittal sinus. When the brain moves relative to the skull in acceleration and deceleration, these veins stretch and tear. Brain atrophy in older adults and in chronic alcohol use lengthens and tenses them, so minor trauma suffices; anticoagulation adds risk. In shaken infants, violent rotation tears them, often with retinal hemorrhages. Low-pressure bleeding spreads freely along the hemisphere, crossing sutures as a crescent, but it is stopped by dural reflections such as the falx and tentorium, so it does not cross the midline. Acute subdural hematoma follows major trauma and often accompanies brain contusion. A chronic subdural hematoma develops over weeks; granulation tissue and fragile new vessels in its membranes rebleed, causing headache, confusion, or slowly progressive deficits that can be mistaken for dementia.

blocks.title: Epidural versus subdural hematoma
rows: Acceleration and deceleration; minor trauma in atrophy
Young adult after a blow to the side of the head
Older adult, chronic alcohol use, shaken infant
Crescent, crosses sutures, not the midline
Bright when acute, about isodense at 1 to 3 weeks, dark when chronic
blocks.caption: Arterial blood under high pressure confined by sutures versus venous blood under low pressure spreading freely.

blocks.title: Localizing an expanding epidural hematoma
blocks.text: A 22-year-old is struck on the left temple, loses consciousness briefly, then talks normally for two hours before becoming drowsy. His left pupil is dilated and unreactive, and his right arm and leg are weak. The lucid interval and temporal blow suggest an epidural hematoma from the left middle meningeal artery. The expanding clot pushes the left uncus over the tentorial edge, compressing the left oculomotor nerve, whose superficial parasympathetic fibers are affected first, so the pupil dilates before the eye deviates. The uncus also compresses the left cerebral peduncle, whose corticospinal fibers cross below in the medulla, causing right-sided weakness.

sections.title: Subarachnoid hemorrhage from a saccular aneurysm

blocks.text: Trauma is the most common cause of subarachnoid blood, but most spontaneous cases come from rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm. About 90% of these aneurysms arise in the anterior circulation, most often at the junction of the anterior communicating artery with the anterior cerebral artery. Other common sites are the MCA bifurcation and the origin of the posterior communicating artery, where an aneurysm can compress the oculomotor nerve and dilate the pupil.

Saccular aneurysms are acquired over life rather than present at birth. At branch points the tunica media is thin or absent, and the internal elastic lamina is fragmented; where flow strikes the apex of a bifurcation, hemodynamic stress gradually balloons the weak wall outward. Within the sac, the wall is thickened hyalinized intima and adventitia without media. Risk rises with conditions that weaken the vessel wall or raise wall stress: autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (defective type III collagen), coarctation of the aorta, smoking, hypertension, and a family history.

Rupture drives arterial blood into the CSF around the brain. Intracranial pressure rises abruptly, producing a sudden, severe headache described as the worst of the patient's life, often with vomiting and brief loss of consciousness. Blood irritates the meninges, causing neck stiffness. CT shows blood in the basal cisterns. If CT is negative, lumbar puncture shows many red cells that do not clear from the first tube to the last, and xanthochromia: red cells lyse, and macrophages convert heme to bilirubin, which colors the supernatant yellow after several hours (reliably by about 12 hours). A traumatic tap gives red cells that decrease across tubes and clear supernatant.

blocks.title: Aneurysm rupture and its complications
steps: Thin media at a branch point balloons into a sac
Rupture fills the subarachnoid space with arterial blood
Thunderclap headache, meningismus, xanthochromic CSF
First day: highest risk of rebleeding
About days 3 to 14: vasospasm causes delayed ischemic infarcts
Blood blocks arachnoid granulations: communicating hydrocephalus
blocks.caption: Complications follow a time course, so the day after rupture predicts which one is most likely.

blocks.text: The complications follow from blood in the CSF. Rebleeding from the unsecured aneurysm is most likely in the first day. Vasospasm develops over about days 3 to 14, peaking near the end of the first week: oxyhemoglobin and its breakdown products scavenge nitric oxide, increase endothelin, and stimulate smooth muscle contraction, narrowing arteries bathed in clot and causing delayed ischemic infarcts. Blood products also clog the arachnoid granulations, impairing CSF absorption and causing communicating hydrocephalus, while clot within the ventricles can obstruct flow. Hyponatremia from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting may also follow.

sections.title: Hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage and cerebral amyloid angiopathy

blocks.text: In intraparenchymal hemorrhage, location usually identifies the cause: deep bleeds point to chronic hypertension, and superficial lobar bleeds in an older adult point to cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Other causes include anticoagulation, arteriovenous malformations (C09), bleeding into tumors, sympathomimetic drugs such as cocaine, and hemorrhagic conversion of infarcts.

Hypertensive hemorrhage arises from the same small penetrating arteries that cause lacunes (C01). Years of high pressure produce hyaline arteriolosclerosis and degeneration of smooth muscle in the media. The weakened wall can either narrow and occlude, producing a lacune, or dilate into Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms, tiny outpouchings of vessels less than about 300 micrometers in diameter, and rupture. The usual sites, in order of frequency in most series, are the putamen and basal ganglia, the thalamus, the pons, and the cerebellar hemispheres. The arterial bleed can keep expanding over the first hours, raising intracranial pressure. Survivors are left with a slit-like cavity lined by hemosiderin-laden macrophages and gliosis.

The deficit reflects the structures in the path. A putaminal hemorrhage compresses the adjacent internal capsule and causes contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss. A thalamic bleed causes contralateral sensory loss and can extend into the third ventricle. A pontine hemorrhage disrupts the reticular activating system and descending tracts, producing coma, quadriparesis, and pinpoint pupils because descending sympathetic fibers are cut while parasympathetic pupillary tone is preserved. A cerebellar hemorrhage causes ataxia, vertigo, and vomiting and is dangerous because it can compress the fourth ventricle and brainstem in the confined posterior fossa.

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is deposition of beta-amyloid, the same peptide found in Alzheimer plaques, in the walls of small and medium arteries of the leptomeninges and cortex. The amyloid replaces smooth muscle, leaving rigid, brittle vessels that stain with Congo red and show apple-green birefringence under polarized light. These vessels lie near the surface, so bleeds are lobar (cortical and subcortical), most often parietal and occipital, and tend to recur in different lobes; small cortical microbleeds accumulate as well. CAA is mainly a disease of older adults, often coexists with Alzheimer disease, and is more likely in carriers of the APOE e4 and e2 alleles.

blocks.title: Deep versus lobar intraparenchymal hemorrhage
rows: Lobar, cortex and subcortical white matter
Older adult, often with cognitive decline
blocks.caption: Location predicts cause because the two diseases damage different vessels.

sections.title: Spinal cord blood supply and anterior spinal artery syndrome

blocks.text: Three longitudinal arteries supply the spinal cord. A single anterior spinal artery, formed by branches of both vertebral arteries, runs in the anterior median fissure and supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord through central (sulcal) branches. Two posterior spinal arteries, from the vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar arteries, supply the posterior third, mainly the dorsal columns and the back of the dorsal horns. Below the cervical cord these vessels are too small to carry blood the whole length of the cord, so they depend on segmental medullary (radicular) arteries that arrive along spinal nerve roots from the vertebral, intercostal, and lumbar arteries.

The largest reinforcing vessel is the great anterior segmental medullary artery (artery of Adamkiewicz). It usually arises on the left from a lower posterior intercostal or upper lumbar artery, most often between about T9 and T12, and it supplies much of the lower thoracic and lumbosacral cord. The mid-thoracic cord, between the cervical supply and this artery, receives few feeders and is a vascular border zone.

blocks.title: Spinal arteries and the structures they supply
rows: Anterior horns, lateral and anterior columns (corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts), autonomic pathways
Paralysis, pain and temperature loss, bladder and bowel dysfunction
Lower thoracic and lumbosacral cord via the anterior spinal artery
Infarction of the lower cord with anterior cord syndrome
blocks.caption: The single anterior artery supplies most of the cord, which is why anterior infarction is far more common than posterior infarction.

blocks.text: Anterior spinal artery syndrome follows interruption of flow to the anterior two-thirds of the cord. The classic causes are aortic surgery with cross-clamping, aortic dissection that shears off intercostal origins, and severe hypotension; atherosclerosis and embolism are less common causes. Onset is sudden, often with back pain. Below the lesion, loss of the lateral corticospinal tracts causes bilateral paralysis, flaccid at first (spinal shock) and later spastic with hyperreflexia and Babinski signs, while loss of the anterior horn cells at the infarcted segments causes lower motor neuron weakness at that level. Loss of the spinothalamic tracts removes pain and temperature sensation bilaterally below the lesion, and loss of descending autonomic pathways causes urinary retention and bowel dysfunction. The dorsal columns, supplied by the posterior arteries, are spared, so vibration and joint position sense remain.

blocks.title: Reading a spinal cord infarct
blocks.text: A 70-year-old wakes after repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm unable to move his legs. He cannot feel pinprick or cold below the umbilicus, and his bladder is distended, yet he feels a tuning fork at both great toes and knows when they are moved up or down. Bilateral motor and spinothalamic loss with intact dorsal columns places the lesion in the anterior two-thirds of the cord. The umbilicus is the T10 dermatome, matching loss of flow through the artery of Adamkiewicz, whose intercostal origin was excluded during aortic clamping.

Vascular malformations are developmental errors in how arteries, capillaries, and veins connect. They are a leading cause of intracerebral hemorrhage and new seizures in children and young adults, in whom hypertension and amyloid angiopathy are unlikely.

An arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is a tangle of abnormal vessels, the nidus, in which arteries drain directly into veins with no capillary bed between them. Without the high resistance of arterioles and capillaries, flow through the shunt is fast and arterial pressure is transmitted into the draining veins. These veins become dilated and arterialized but remain thin-walled, so they can rupture, causing intraparenchymal hemorrhage, sometimes with subarachnoid or intraventricular extension. The low-resistance shunt can also divert flow from surrounding brain (steal), and the gliotic, hemosiderin-stained tissue between the vessels is irritable, so seizures are a common first sign. AVMs most often present between about 10 and 30 years of age, are more common in males, and arise most often in the MCA territory. A bruit may be heard over the skull. Multiple AVMs, including in the lung and liver, suggest hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, an autosomal dominant disorder of TGF-beta signaling genes.
Other malformations differ in flow and in whether brain tissue lies between the vessels, which determines their behavior.

blocks.title: Cerebral vascular malformations compared
rows: Arteries draining directly to veins, gliotic brain between vessels
Hemorrhage and seizures in young adults
Packed thin-walled sinusoidal channels, no brain between them, hemosiderin rim
Seizures and small recurrent bleeds; may be familial (CCM genes)
Dilated capillaries separated by normal brain, often in the pons
blocks.caption: Flow and the presence or absence of intervening brain explain why AVMs bleed most dangerously.

blocks.text: Ectatic cerebral vessels are elongated, dilated, and tortuous arteries, most often the basilar artery (dolichoectasia), usually in older adults with long-standing hypertension and atherosclerosis. They cause symptoms by compressing cranial nerves or brainstem, or by allowing thrombus to form in slow, disturbed flow.

sections.title: Cervical artery dissection and subclavian steal

blocks.text: Dissection of the internal carotid or vertebral artery is one of the most common causes of stroke in young and middle-aged adults. A tear in the intima lets blood enter the media, forming an intramural hematoma. The hematoma can narrow or occlude the lumen, but stroke more often results from thrombus that forms on the exposed subintimal surface and embolizes downstream. Triggers range from obvious trauma to minor neck movements such as sports, sudden rotation, or neck manipulation. Underlying wall weakness from fibromuscular dysplasia, vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, or Marfan syndrome increases risk.

Internal carotid dissection usually causes pain in the neck, face, or around the eye, and an ipsilateral partial Horner syndrome. The third-order sympathetic fibers to the eye run in the plexus on the internal carotid wall, so the expanding wall injures them, causing ptosis and miosis. Facial sweating is usually spared because the sudomotor fibers to most of the face travel with the external carotid artery. Emboli then reach the MCA territory. Vertebral dissection, often where the artery winds around the atlas, causes posterior neck or occipital pain followed by posterior circulation ischemia, classically the lateral medullary syndrome.

Subclavian steal is a reversal of flow in a vertebral artery. When the subclavian artery is stenosed or occluded proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery, usually by atherosclerosis and more often on the left, pressure in the distal subclavian falls below pressure at the basilar junction. Blood then flows up the opposite vertebral artery, across the basilar junction, and down the vertebral artery on the stenosed side to supply the arm. Exercising the arm lowers its resistance and increases the reversed flow, which can briefly reduce brainstem perfusion.

blocks.title: Subclavian steal
steps: Stenosis of subclavian artery before the vertebral origin
Pressure in distal subclavian falls below basilar pressure
Flow reverses down the ipsilateral vertebral artery
Arm exercise lowers arm resistance and increases reversed flow
Arm claudication, weak pulse, lower blood pressure on that side
Dizziness, vertigo, or syncope from vertebrobasilar insufficiency
blocks.caption: The arm draws blood from the posterior circulation because the stenosis lowers pressure in its own supply.

blocks.text: Findings follow from the pressure drop: systolic pressure lower by more than about 15 to 20 mm Hg in the affected arm, a weaker radial pulse, and sometimes a supraclavicular bruit. Many patients are asymptomatic because collateral flow compensates. Takayasu arteritis is a cause in young women.

sections.title: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, hypertensive encephalopathy, and PRES

blocks.text: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is clotting in the dural venous sinuses, most often the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses, or in the cortical veins that drain into them. It follows Virchow's triad. Hypercoagulable states dominate: pregnancy and especially the postpartum period, estrogen-containing contraceptives, inherited thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A mutation, antiphospholipid syndrome, and malignancy. Dehydration and nearby infection, such as mastoiditis spreading to the sigmoid and transverse sinuses, contribute through stasis and local inflammation. It affects younger adults, women more than men.

Obstructed outflow raises venous and capillary pressure upstream. Fluid leaks into the brain, capillaries rupture, and the result is edema and hemorrhagic venous infarcts that do not match any arterial territory and are often bilateral and parasagittal when the superior sagittal sinus is blocked. Because the arachnoid granulations drain CSF into the sinuses, absorption also falls, so intracranial pressure rises. Headache is the most common symptom, often with papilledema, vomiting, and sometimes abducens palsy; seizures are more common than in arterial stroke because venous infarcts involve cortex and contain blood. Contrast imaging may show a filling defect within the sinus.

Hypertensive encephalopathy and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) are failures of autoregulation. Cerebral arterioles normally hold flow nearly constant across a mean arterial pressure of about 60 to 150 mm Hg by constricting as pressure rises; chronic hypertension shifts this range upward. When pressure rises suddenly above the upper limit, the constriction is overcome, arterioles are forcibly dilated, and the capillary bed is exposed to high pressure. The blood-brain barrier leaks and vasogenic edema forms. The posterior circulation is affected most, probably because vertebrobasilar arterioles receive less sympathetic innervation to limit dilation. In severe hypertensive encephalopathy, fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles and petechial hemorrhages appear.

blocks.title: Autoregulatory breakthrough in PRES
steps: Sudden severe hypertension or endothelial injury
Pressure exceeds the upper limit of autoregulation
Arterioles are forcibly dilated; capillary pressure rises
Blood-brain barrier leaks plasma into the interstitium
Vasogenic edema of parieto-occipital white matter
Headache, confusion, visual loss, seizures; usually reversible
blocks.caption: The edema is extracellular and reversible if the cause is removed before infarction or hemorrhage develops.

blocks.text: PRES also occurs without extreme pressure when the endothelium is injured, as in preeclampsia and eclampsia, renal failure, and exposure to calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) or cytotoxic chemotherapy. Patients have headache, confusion, visual disturbance up to cortical blindness, and seizures. MRI shows bright T2 and FLAIR signal in the parieto-occipital white matter that typically resolves, distinguishing it from infarction.

blocks.title: Cytotoxic versus vasogenic edema
rows: ATP and Na+/K+ ATPase failure; cells swell
Blood-brain barrier leak; fluid in interstitium
Gray and white matter of the injured territory
In ischemia, usually marks dying cells
blocks.caption: Infarcts begin with cytotoxic edema and add vasogenic edema as capillaries fail; PRES is primarily vasogenic.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology predict nearly every lesion in this chapter. Arterial territories decide the deficit of an infarct, the ends of those territories decide where hypotension strikes, the dura and its sutures shape extra-axial bleeds, and the single anterior spinal artery explains why the dorsal columns survive cord infarction. Cerebral autoregulation explains why the brain tolerates a wide range of pressures and why both very low pressure (watershed infarcts) and very high pressure (PRES) cause injury. Biochemistry supplies the shared cell death pathway: ATP failure, glutamate excitotoxicity, and Ca2+ overload explain why CA1 and Purkinje neurons die first.

Pathology links the vessel wall to the outcome. Hypertension produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis that ends either in a lacune or a Charcot-Bouchard rupture at the same deep sites, atherosclerosis produces thrombosis and artery-to-artery emboli, and connective tissue and genetic disorders such as ADPKD, vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia explain aneurysms and malformations in young patients. The limits are worth keeping in mind: CT is insensitive to early ischemia, the time course of an infarct varies with its size, and examination alone cannot separate ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke.

summary: Thrombotic infarcts arise on atherosclerotic plaques at the carotid bifurcation, MCA, or basilar artery; embolic infarcts come mainly from the heart, are maximal at onset, and often turn hemorrhagic when flow returns.
Lacunes are small deep infarcts from hypertensive hyaline arteriolosclerosis of penetrating arteries, causing pure motor or pure sensory strokes.
An infarct evolves from red neurons at about 12 to 24 hours to neutrophils, foamy macrophages over weeks, and finally a cyst walled by gliosis from liquefactive necrosis.
About 85% of strokes are ischemic; a TIA leaves no infarct; noncontrast CT comes first because acute blood is immediately bright while early ischemia is often invisible.
Global hypoxia kills CA1 pyramidal cells, Purkinje cells, and cortical layers 3, 5, and 6 first through excitotoxicity; hypotension infarcts the ACA and MCA watershed.
Epidural hematoma is arterial, biconvex, limited by sutures, and may show a lucid interval; subdural hematoma is venous, crescentic, and crosses sutures in atrophic or shaken brains.
Saccular aneurysms at the anterior communicating artery cause thunderclap headache and xanthochromia, then rebleeding, vasospasm at about days 3 to 14, and hydrocephalus.
Deep intraparenchymal hemorrhage points to hypertensive Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms; recurrent lobar hemorrhage in older adults points to amyloid angiopathy.
Anterior spinal artery infarction after aortic surgery causes paralysis, pain and temperature loss, and bladder dysfunction with vibration and position sense spared.
AVMs cause hemorrhage and seizures in young adults; dissection causes stroke with neck pain and Horner syndrome; venous sinus thrombosis and PRES cause edema outside arterial territories.

verify: Infarct timing (red neurons 12 to 24 hours, neutrophils 1 to 3 days, macrophages from about day 3, gliosis from about 1 week) varies between Robbins and review sources; values are given as approximate.
The ischemic versus hemorrhagic split is quoted as 80 to 87% ischemic in different sources; this chapter uses about 85%.

Normal cerebral blood flow (about 50 mL per 100 g per minute) and the autoregulatory range (about 60 to 150 mm Hg mean arterial pressure; some texts give 50 to 150 or 60 to 140) differ slightly between Guyton and Hall and other texts.
Time to irreversible neuronal injury in normothermic global ischemia is quoted as about 4 to 6 minutes; confirm the value NABNE expects.
The frequency of a lucid interval in epidural hematoma varies widely between series; it is presented here as occurring in some patients rather than with a percentage.
Time for xanthochromia to appear after subarachnoid hemorrhage is quoted from about 2 to 12 hours; vasospasm window given as about days 3 to 14.
The usual level of origin of the artery of Adamkiewicz is given as about T9 to T12, with a wider range of T8 to L2 in anatomical series.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Sommer sector, Charcot-Bouchard, and artery of Adamkiewicz, or only descriptive terms.
